data.title: Audit Log
data.tagline: An audit log records who did what to which object, when, and with what result.
data.learningOutcome: You can tell whether a record is sufficient to investigate a permission change and distinguish audit logs from errors and monitoring.
data.description: After an administrator changes the billing-editor role, an audit log can record the actor, time, target, action, and success or denial so the permission change can be investigated. It is different from an error log that explains a program failure and from monitoring that observes health signals; request data may contain sensitive information, so its scope and access need control.

learning.assumes: You know an administrator's action can change an account, permission, or resource state.
learning.outcome: You can tell whether a record is sufficient to investigate a permission change and distinguish audit logs from errors and monitoring.

explanation.title: Make the action visible
explanation.text: Knowing only that the current permission changed is not enough. Connect the actor, time, target, action, and success or denial result so the team can reconstruct the security-relevant operation.

explanation.title: Return investigation to the permission flow
explanation.text: If a member suddenly loses checkout access, filter records by account, role, and time, then check whether the request succeeded and which identity source was involved. Fix the cause and verify a new searchable record; without accessible records, the sequence cannot be reconstructed reliably.

explanation.title: A second scenario: correcting a medical record
explanation.text: When a medical record is corrected, the audit log should connect the actor, time, target record, change, and result so the team can reconstruct who changed what. Unrelated sensitive content should not be copied into the log in full.

data.boundary: An audit log tracks who did what to which object for accountability; an error log explains where a program failed; monitoring observes health signals such as error rate and latency. Auditing is not logging everything: request bodies may contain passwords, tokens, or personal data, so fields, retention, and access must be controlled.

lessonPractice.title: Someone removed a finance-team member's checkout permission. Which evidence should you use first?

options.label: Find an audit record with the actor, time, target permission, action, and result
options.feedback: Correct. An audit record puts the key facts of a security-relevant action into one traceable piece of evidence.

options.label: Search only server error logs; no error means no permission changed
options.feedback: A permission change can succeed without an error, and an error log usually does not identify who intentionally made the change.

options.label: Use the day's request-volume chart to infer which administrator acted from the peak
options.feedback: Request volume shows counts, not the actor, target permission, action, or result.

data.agentPrompt: Add audit logging for administrator permission changes. Record at least the actor, time, target account or role, action, and success or denial result. Do not write passwords or unnecessary sensitive content to the log. Verify one successful and one denied change, show that both records are searchable, and state who can access them.
